description: Applications and binary data, standards organizations (IETF, IEEE, ISO), OSI vs. TCP/IP vs. Equivalent 5-layer model, core protocols across all 5 layers, and end-to-end encapsulation & decapsulation.

lessons.title: Applications, Data & Standards
lessons.summary: See how user information becomes 0s and 1s, trace a web request end-to-end, and distinguish IETF, IEEE, and ISO.

lessons.title: OSI vs. TCP/IP Reference Models
lessons.sectionTitle: Network Reference Models and Standard Protocols
lessons.summary: Compare the 7-layer OSI model, the 4-layer TCP/IP model, and the 5-layer Equivalent TCP/IP model plus PDUs at every layer.

lessons.title: Application & Transport Layers
lessons.sectionTitle: Network Reference Models and Standard Protocols
lessons.summary: Master well-known TCP/UDP ports (HTTP 80, DNS 53, Telnet 23, FTP 20/21, SMTP 25), DNS resolution, HTTP C/S flow, and TCP vs. UDP.

lessons.title: Network Layer & IP Packet Forwarding
lessons.sectionTitle: Network Reference Models and Standard Protocols
lessons.summary: Learn how IPv4/IPv6 logical addressing, routing tables, next hops, OSPF/BGP, and ICMP work together to move packets across networks.

lessons.title: Data Link (Ethernet/PPP) & Physical Media
lessons.sectionTitle: Network Reference Models and Standard Protocols
lessons.summary: Study Ethernet & 48-bit MAC addresses, CSMA/CD history, PPP negotiation (LCP -> Auth -> NCP), and twisted pair, fiber, hybrid cables & Wi-Fi.

lessons.title: Encapsulation, Decapsulation & Quiz
lessons.summary: Walk step-by-step through sender encapsulation, Layer 2 switching vs. Layer 3 routing in transit, receiver decapsulation, and the official Quiz.

challenge.prompt: Match each standards organization to its landmark networking contribution (Slide 9):

pairs.right: Develops TCP/IP Internet protocols and publishes RFCs

challenge.explanation: IETF publishes RFCs for TCP/IP, IEEE standardizes Ethernet (802.3) and Wi-Fi (802.11), and ISO published the OSI model.

challenge.prompt: Match each layer of the Equivalent TCP/IP model to its official Protocol Data Unit (PDU) name (Slides 13–26):
challenge.explanation: Top to bottom PDUs in HCIA-Datacom: Application -> Data, Transport -> Segment, Network -> Packet, Data Link -> Frame, Physical -> Bitstream.

challenge.prompt: Fill in the standard transport protocols and port numbers from Slide 14:
challenge.template: HTTP uses TCP port [0], Telnet uses TCP port [1], SMTP uses TCP port [2], and DNS uses UDP port [3].
challenge.explanation: Memorize these HCIA staple ports: HTTP = 80 (TCP), SMTP = 25 (TCP), Telnet = 23 (TCP), FTP = 20 & 21 (TCP), DNS = 53 (UDP).

challenge.prompt: Which scenarios are best suited for UDP rather than TCP? (Slides 17–18)
options: Real-time video calls where low latency matters more than retransmitting lost packets
File transfer requiring guaranteed zero-loss, in-order delivery
Online gaming traffic tolerant of minor packet loss
challenge.explanation: UDP (RFC 768) is connectionless with ultra-low overhead and latency — ideal for video calls, online gaming, and DNS queries. File transfers and web browsing use reliable TCP (RFC 793).

challenge.prompt: When an intermediate router receives an IP packet, what does it look up to decide the next hop and outbound interface? (Slide 20)
options: The destination MAC address in its local ARP table
The destination IP address in its routing table
The destination TCP port number in its session table
challenge.explanation: Routers inspect the destination IP address in the network-layer header and search their routing table (like a map) for a matching entry specifying the next hop and outbound interface.

challenge.prompt: Order the three negotiation stages of PPP link establishment from first to last (Slide 25):
items: LCP negotiation (Establish phase: MRU, working mode, auth method)
challenge.explanation: PPP always negotiates link parameters first with LCP, optionally authenticates via CHAP or PAP, and finally negotiates network-layer parameters (like IP addresses) via NCP/IPCP.

challenge.prompt: Which statement about transmission media is TRUE according to Slide 27?
options: Cat 5e/Cat 6 twisted pair cables with RJ45 connectors support a maximum transmission distance of 100 m
Multimode fiber has less dispersion and larger capacity than single-mode fiber for long-distance links
Hybrid cable 2.0 requires separate RJ45 electrical and LC optical ports on the switch
UTP cables are more expensive and harder to bend than STP cables
challenge.explanation: Twisted pair Cat 5/5e/6 cables with RJ45 connectors have a 100 m max distance. Single-mode fiber (not multimode) is for long-distance, UTP is cheaper/lighter than STP, and Hybrid cable 2.0 uses a single hybrid port.

challenge.prompt: Trace Data Encapsulation on the Sender when a browser loads www.huawei.com (Slide 29):
items: Transport layer adds TCP Header -> Segment
Network layer adds IP Header -> Packet
Data Link layer adds Eth Header & FCS Trailer -> Frame
Physical layer converts Frame into Bitstream over media
challenge.explanation: Encapsulation proceeds top-down: Data -> TCP Segment -> IP Packet -> Ethernet Frame (with Eth Header + FCS trailer) -> Physical Bitstream.
